book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band

chapters.relation: Wrathall's introduction argues U2 is philosophically interesting because its enormous popularity holds up a mirror to what 'we' care about (by Nietzsche's test of how a culture stands toward life) and because the band publicly wrestles with the contradictions of the technological-global economy: unprecedented freedom of choice paired with loss of rooted identity, and distant suffering ('Crumbs from Your Table') that we feel both powerless to fix and responsible for. Its showcase reading treats 'Miracle Drug' as a musical theodicy: Bono's plea 'God, I need your help tonight' is answered by the Edge's guitar and by the Matthew 25:35 refrain, so science and medicine count as works of Christian charity. The piece then frames the volume's essays: Plato's ascent of love in the early songs, Kierkegaardian despair after Achtung Baby, Bono's search for authentic identity, the simulacra of 'Even Better than the Real Thing', being-toward-death in the apocalyptic songs, and the Plato-versus-Aristotle quarrel over music's emotional power.

McCoy reads U2's early longing songs through the Symposium: Aristophanes' split-beings myth turns 'New Year's Day' into a song about incompleteness whose separated lovers also stand for Poland under Soviet domination, and Diotima's ladder of love reads 'I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For' and 'City of Blinding Lights' as stages ascending from bodily beauty toward the soul and then to Beauty itself. Against a tragic reading, she argues that by Diotima's account the restless lover on the ascent 'begets' discourses and songs, so 'With or Without You' is a song of surrender rather than despair. October's 'Gloria' and 'With a Shout' get the Augustinian ending: the restless heart finds in God the object Romantic love never supplies.

Dreyfus and Wrathall read U2's head/heart split through Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death: the Christian-Platonic strategy of escaping the earthly (the sun-blindness of 'Staring at the Sun', the ascent of 'Gone') collapses into despair once both sides of the self prove essential, while 'The Playboy Mansion' and 'Discotheque' depict Kierkegaardian leveling and spiritlessness in consumer culture and 'Last Night on Earth' the aesthetic-sphere despair of living pure possibility. Pascal's contradictory great-and-miserable self and Augustine's two cities supply the tradition U2 inherits, and Nietzsche's 'nihilism' names what U2 calls 'pop'. They close by arguing that Bono's pseudonymous stage characters (the Fly, MacPhisto) do phenomenology just as Kierkegaard's pseudonyms do, and that U2's songs about something missing bear out despair's 'dialectic of eternity'.

Wrathall reads 'Vertigo' through Heidegger's vertigo-before-a-question and Kierkegaard's account of despair as the dizziness of a self whose sensual and spiritual sides are both essential. He uses rock's own testimony - Rammstein's 'Engel' and 'Sehnsucht', Nine Inch Nails' 'Down in It' - to confirm the existentialist thesis that neither flesh nor spirit can be renounced, with Pascal's God-shaped void as the diagnosis. He then argues that 'Beautiful Day', 'When I Look at the World', 'Grace' and 'Mysterious Ways' sketch an existential Christianity in which faith is not propositional confidence but a world-disclosing skill acquired like any know-how, and in which concrete erotic love ('if you want to kiss the sky, better learn how to kneel', the girl with crimson nails who 'has Jesus round her neck') discloses God on earth.

Malpas takes The Joshua Tree as an album about place: its desert imagery and restless movement ('Where the Streets Have No Name', 'I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For' as 'an anthem of doubt more than faith') carry the listener from Ireland to Reagan's America to Pinochet's Chile, while its political references - Ethiopian famine, El Salvador, Dublin high-rises - always work through concrete locations rather than abstract ideals. Using Heidegger on homelessness as the inability to dwell, and Marx and Engels' 'all that is solid melts into air', he argues that modernity has not erased our relatedness to place but covered it over. The album's desolation is therefore readable the other way: belonging is constituted through care, commitment and uncertain journeying in the places we already are ('Heartland').

Soper tracks Bono's public identity work across three paradigms: pre-modern Irish-Catholic inheritance, including a Du Boisian 'double consciousness' of the colonized Irish; the modernist artist-as-visionary, where Nietzsche, Freud and Marx destabilize the self and the Shalom fellowship nearly ends the band; and the postmodern masks of the Fly, Mirrorball Man and MacPhisto on the Zoo TV media collage, read via Lacan for 'Mofo' and via Baudrillard's simulacra for the 'Even Better than the Real Thing' video with its wax Beatles and cyber-sex imagery. Lyotardian skepticism toward grand ideologies explains the band's refusal of fanaticism in 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' and 'Two Hearts Beat as One'. Soper concludes that Bono fuses all three into a 'Postmodern Christian Pragmatism' that keeps Christian conviction and debt-relief activism while adopting postmodern playfulness without collapsing into ironic detachment.

Thomson uses U2's self-declared postmodern phase to define postmodernity itself: a sensitivity to poetic polysemy against modernity's fantasies of total control (Heidegger's reduction of everything to optimizable resource), Lyotard's incredulity toward metanarratives - defended against the self-refutation charge and narrowed to the dying metanarratives of unity and emancipation - and the Marx-Nietzsche-Freud hermeneutics of suspicion that fragmented the subject, with Kierkegaard and early Heidegger as the resisters. Derrida's 9/11 analysis of autoimmunity and hauntology is read into 'Peace on Earth' and the sorrows that 'learned to swim' in 'Until the End of the World'. The payoff is a polysemic reading of 'Even Better than the Real Thing': risky as a seeming hymn to Baudrillard's simulacra, addressed to a live audience it celebrates a communal love 'even better' than personal love - Diotima's ladder generalized - making the postmodern U2 continuous with the 'Christ-ian' U2 of universal love, sealed by 'One'.

Merrick sets XTC's 'Dear God' - being 'just struck' that no loving, all-powerful God rules this world - against U2's laments ('Wake Up Dead Man', 'Peace on Earth', '40') and Bono's reading of the Psalms as the blues shouted at God: both share outrage, but U2 adds yearning for the redemption promised in 'the story about eternity' plus Jubilee 2000-style action against debt and AIDS. He then argues the atheistic reaction to evil cannot be reason-producing, since neither divine design nor unguided evolution would give us a faculty that 'just sees' atheism from evil, any more than one that just sees there is no plant life on Mars. If God instead made us so that outrage at evil can trigger conviction that he will make all right, U2's reaction - 'Grace makes beauty out of ugly things' - can be as reasonable as visual perception.

The authors apply Gilligan's and Noddings' ethics of care to U2: 'Bad' shows the speaker as Noddings' 'one-caring', and 'Sometimes You Can't Make It on Your Own' - Bono caring for his dying father through anger and resentment - exemplifies care's insistence on the particular relationship over universal rules, refusing abstraction even of the usual songwriting metaphors. 'Peace on Earth' names the Omagh bomb's dead (Sean, Julia, Gareth, Ann, Breda) and 'Van Diemen's Land' refuses both IRA and British sides, showing care ethics rejecting the utilitarian accounting and the Kantian universalizability arguments that could rationalize such violence. They conclude U2 are philosophical rather than political feminists: Gilligan's 'different voice' is not a woman's voice, and the band's connected knowing - debt relief sung as connection in 'Beautiful Day' - makes maternal thinking 'loud, rhythmic, catchy, even cool'.

Delancey asks why anyone should take moral and political cues from a rock band and answers via Heidegger: in a mediascape where a few corporations orchestrate what everyone hears, the mass tune is das Man ('Numb'), and adopting it is inauthenticity - so U2, who believe what they sing for their own reasons ('Mothers of the Disappeared' against the official line on Latin America), may be among the most authentic voices available. Plato's tripartite soul and Aristotle's golden mean supply the thesis that reason needs rightly trained passion: the righteous anger of 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' and 'Silver and Gold' and the resolve of 'Walk On' are practical wisdom in song, the emotions democracy requires. Against Plato's philosopher-king and his noble lies, Delancey argues utopia can only be fostered, not enforced - so in a democracy, if you want to change the world, you may have to sing to people.

Benfell reads U2's apocalyptic songs through Heidegger rather than through eschatological doctrine: 'The Playboy Mansion' depicts fallenness in the 'they', a consumerist paradise with 'no time for sorrow' that lets us flee our own death, while the angel's fall in Wenders' films evoked by 'Stay' and the day-to-day constraints of 'Some Days Are Better than Others' illustrate thrownness, and 'Gone' existential guilt as an unpayable debt. A verse-by-verse reading of 'Until the End of the World' - the Judas-at-the-last-supper reading as one register - shows the speaker moving from 'passing time' and playing roles in the 'they' to anxious guiltiness and the call of conscience, reaching for the one whose resolute waiting models anticipatory resoluteness. The 'end of the world', he concludes, is the end of the speaker's own world: U2's apocalyptic imagery calls listeners to authentic, finite existence, not to prediction of last things.

Han-Pile tests three traditional philosophies of music against U2's own talk about music: the rationalist (Descartes and Leibniz's 'unconscious exercise of arithmetic', satirized by Hit Song Science finding U2 mathematically close to Beethoven), the subjectivist (Hegel and Wackenroder on music as the expression of inner feeling, mirrored in Bono's method of articulating in words the feeling the band first found in improvisation), and the metaphysical (the Pythagorean-Boethian musica mundana whose harmony with our music 'Gloria' and 'Wake Up Dead Man' both invoke, consummated in Schopenhauer's music as direct copy of the will, which Nietzsche's critique of Wagner undermines). Against all three she sets Heidegger's Stimmung: music discloses shared moods - atmospheres that color how a whole world shows up, as 'Beautiful Day' or 'Bullet the Blue Sky' demonstrate. U2's vocation is thus to shift the numbed basic disposition of the age ('Zooropa', 'Numb') toward joy and compassion - rock 'n' roll as an alarm clock for 'dreaming up the world we want to live in'.

Gracyk explains U2's two commercial breakthroughs by pitting expression theory against Austin-style speech act theory: songs succeed not through verifiable autobiographical sincerity - 'Stuck in a Moment' was written about Michael Hutchence's suicide yet became the song of post-9/11 America, and 'I Will Follow' outmoves its equally sincere siblings - but because singing to an audience is an indirect illocutionary act that suspends ordinary commitments and invites listeners to make the song relevant to their own lives, as 'With or Without You' does by staying focused yet open-ended. Wittgenstein's point that an utterance's meaning depends on the actions into which it is woven frames the view that the audience must complete the speech act, as Larry Mullen does when he fits Dylan's 'With God on Our Side' to Northern Ireland. Pop failed, Gracyk argues, because 'Discotheque' and 'The Playboy Mansion' lecture - talk to the audience about consumerism rather than talking through them - so the unspoken invitation was withdrawn.

Cleveland sorts the knowing and feeling of U2's lyrics ('Vertigo', 'Beautiful Day', 'Staring at the Sun', 'Daddy's Gonna Pay for Your Crash Car') into Russell's varieties of knowledge - propositional, acquaintance, know-how - and argues that the feeling U2 champions against thought is knowledge by acquaintance: direct, concept-free awareness that, in religious cases, just is Jamesian mystical revelation as against revelation as a set of propositional truths, which is why Bono tells his father he 'hears something back from the silence' rather than holding doctrines. James supplies both the view that feeling is the deeper source of religion and the pragmatist answer to the problem of origins - 'by their fruits ye shall know them', so religious feeling is vindicated by moral transformation. Hume's slave-of-the-passions thesis explains why such feeling, not inert moral knowledge, moves Bono's social justice work: 'God is love, and as much as I respond... in acting in that love, that's my religion'.

Tollefsen revives Plato's ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry: artistic imitations, three removes from the Forms and aimed at the soul's emotional part, stir 'imitative emotions' - purer, shorter-lived, effort-free surrogates for the real labors of love, faith and community - and he builds a four-stage account of the U2 formula (idealized transcendent love in the lyrics, religious imagery fusing lover and God, the Edge's Big Music crescendo, and the concert 'you' extended to the crowd, as in the Elevation-tour 'I Will Follow' with its 'Amazing Grace' bells) to show U2 are masters of exactly this seduction. The healing fans felt after September 11th may therefore be an image of redemption rather than the reality. Where Aristotle and Aquinas would educate the emotions rather than suppress them, Tollefsen's quarrel is with imitation itself; his verdict is that U2 suffer from Misplaced Artistic Pretension - high imagery where honest trash (or genuine complexity) would do.

Werther answers Tollefsen with Aristotle's Politics: musical images of character effect real 'change[s] of soul', so a three-premise argument concludes that repeated exposure to U2's images of fine character and good action can habituate delight in virtue - King's courage in 'Pride (In the Name of Love)' (whatever the botched time of day, and as proved when Adam Clayton stepped between Bono and an FBI-confirmed death threat), the indignation and shame at global poverty in 'Crumbs from Your Table', and the compassion of 'Miracle Drug' for the locked-in writer Christopher Nolan. 'Exit' purges the band's demons and 'Until the End of the World' offers purification through holy fear, matching the medical and religious readings of Aristotelian catharsis. C.S. Lewis's Abolition of Man closes the case: without the aid of trained emotions the intellect is powerless, so a culture raised on U2's feelings may be better prepared to act well than one raised on syllogisms alone.

holes.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
holes.what: Russian novelist-philosopher of existential Christianity whose underground man dramatizes self-despising despair and whose Father Zosima preaches faith confirmed by active love.
holes.why: Chapter 12 reads 'Mysterious Ways' through Notes from Underground and grounds its account of faith's confirmation in Zosima's 'experience of active love' from The Brothers Karamazov; chapter 11 also counts Dostoevsky among the existential Christians alongside Pascal and Kierkegaard.

holes.name: Place, Home and Dwelling
holes.what: The account of how human lives are articulated through concrete places, with modernity diagnosed as homelessness - an inability to dwell (Heidegger's later thinking on place and dwelling).
holes.why: Chapter 13 is built entirely on this: The Joshua Tree as an album of place, home, belonging and loss, read through Heidegger on dwelling and Marx's 'all that is solid melts into air', and no existing slug captures the philosophy of place itself.

holes.name: J.L. Austin
holes.what: Ordinary-language philosopher whose speech act theory (How to Do Things with Words) analyzes utterances as actions with locutionary, illocutionary and perlocutionary dimensions completed by cooperative audiences.
holes.why: Chapter 23's entire explanation of U2's popular success - singing as an indirect illocutionary act that invites listeners to make songs relevant to their own lives - is constructed from Austin's distinctions, and Austin appears in the book's index as a principal figure.

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation and purification)
holes.what: Aristotle's notion that tragedy and music work on the emotions of pity and fear, read by commentators either as medical purgation of excess feeling or as religious purification of the soul.
holes.why: Chapter 26 devotes a full section to the two scholarly readings of catharsis, mapping 'Exit' onto purgation and 'Until the End of the World' onto purification, and no existing slug covers it.

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Twentieth-century Christian philosopher-apologist whose Abolition of Man argues that trained emotions, not syllogisms, are what make virtue psychologically possible.
holes.why: Chapter 26 takes its subtitle from The Abolition of Man and closes its Aristotelian case by quoting Lewis's claim that without the aid of trained emotions the intellect is powerless against the animal organism.
